Bhīmaratha-śānti
(‘propitiatory rite [to counter the effects of] Bhīmarathī’)
------------------------------------------
Śāntis are propitiatory rites performed with a view to countering the evil effects of malevolent spirits, unlucky स्तर्स्, ill-omens including bad द्रेअम्स् or un-favourable deities.
When a person reaches the age of 77 years, 7 months and 7 days, that particular night is called ‘Bhīmarathī’ since it is said to be terrible (bhīma = terrible) and difficult to survive. The rite to be performed to offset its effects is called ‘Bhīmaratha-śānti,’ or ‘Bhimarathī-śānti’.
It may be performed on the completion of the seventieth year itself. Its object is to protect his life as also the lives and properties of all his children and grand-children.
The rite involves several acts like nāndīśrāddha (See ĀBHYUDAYIKA-ŚRĀDDHA.), kalaśasthāpana (ceremonially establishing the holy water pot), worship of deities like भीम-mṛtyuñjaya, दुर्गा, गणपति and विष्णु as also the नवग्रहस् (the nine प्लनेत्स्), chanting of Vedic hymns like the Rudra and the Camaka, the Śrīsūkta and the Bhūsūkta, homas (offering oblations into duly consecrated fires), the main होम being the Mṛtyuñjaya-होम with the well-known hymn, ‘tryambakaṁ yajāmane’ as also an अभिषेक (ceremonial sprinkling of consecrated waters) to the Yajamāna, the performer. He should then give gifts to the prescribed persons, and get the blessings of the priests and the other ब्राह्मणस् involved in the rite.

Bhīma
(‘the terrible one’):
------------------------------------------
The heroes and the villains portrayed in the two epics—the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata—have not only swayed the emotions of the Indian masses for millennia but also kept the ideals before them: the positive ideals or how to be, and the negative ideals or how not to be.
Śrī कृष्ण, भीष्म, विदुर and the Pāṇḍava heroes of the Mahābhārata have provided the positive ideals.
Bhīma, or Bhīmasena the second of the Pāṇḍavas, was not only the very personification of physical prowess but also of fearlessness. Born to कुन्ती, the first wife of the king पाण्डु, by the grace of वायु, the god of wind, भीम was celebrated for his large frame and immense strength equal to that of ‘ten thousand elephants!’All efforts of the wily दुर्योधन, the eldest of the Kauravas, an inveterate enemy of the Pāṇḍavas and especially of Bīma, to liquidate him were set at naught by the latter’s strength aided by divine grace. Feeding with poisonous ड़ोओद्, attack by venomous reptiles and arson were some of the methods tried out by दुर्योधन.
Bhīma was an adept in the art of fighting with the गदा or the mace, in which he had been vigorously trained by बलराम, the elder brother of Śrī कृष्ण. He had been presented with a divine mace by Mayāsura, the chief architect of the असुरस् or demons. Apart from द्रौपदी, the common wife of the Pāṇḍava brothers, भीम had wedded Hiḍimbā and Jalan-dharā. घटोत्कच, another colossus, was his son from Hiḍimbā.
The number of demons and villains killed by भीम was legion: Hiḍimbāsura, Bakāsura, जरासन्ध and कीचक to name a few. He did so under great personal risk but inspired by the desire to protect the good, the meek and the weak.
The crowning success of भीम was achieved when he killed दुश्शासन and दुर्योधन (the eldest of the Kaurava brothers) in the कुरुक्षेत्र war, thus avenging all the wrongs done by them to the Pāṇḍava family.
He was a great source of strength and support to युधिष्ठिर, after the latter was crowned as the emperor at हस्तिनापुर.
In spite of his massive appearance and all his fierce exploits, भीम had a simple and tender heart and was deeply devoted to Śrī कृष्ण.
See also MAHĀBHĀRATA.

Bhīmaikādaśī
(‘ekādaśī [associated with] भीम’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most well-known and popular days of religious observances in the lunar चलेन्दर् of the Hindus, is the एकादशी. It is the eleventh day from the full-मोओन् or the new-मोओन्, each month. It is considered as a ‘vrata’ or a religious observance, characterised mainly by ड़स्तिन्ग्.
(See EKĀDAŚĪ for details.)
Out of the several ekādaśīs considered as even more sacred, भीमैकादशी is one. According to the Matsyapurāṇa. (69.19-65) Śrī कृष्ण is said to have imparted the knowledge of the भीम-dvādaṣī vrata including those rites to be performed on the daśamī (the tenth) and the एकादशी (the eleventh) days to भीम, the second of the Pāṇḍava princes. Hence the names ‘Bhimaikādaśī’ and ‘Bhīmadvādaśī’. They are observed on the eleventh and the twelfth of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha (February), with or without the conjunction of the star पुष्य. The latter day used to be called ‘Kalyāṇinī’ also.
On the tenth day (Māgha śukla daśamī) the votary is expected to take a bath after applying ghee to his body and worship विष्णु with the मन्त्र ‘Oṁ namo nārāyaṇāya’ followed by the worship of गरुड, शिव and गणेश. On the eleventh day (ekādaśī) a total fast is to be observed. On the next day (dvādaśī) he has to bathe in a river, raise a मण्डप or a pavilion in front of his होउसे, hang a jar full of water but with a hole at the bottom, receive the drops of water on his palm repeating the name of God throughout the night and perform होम (offering oblations into a duly consecrated fire) the next morning with the help of twelve priests learned in the वेदस्, honouring them suitably at the end. On the thirteenth day (trayodaśī), 13 cows have to be donated. He should then listen to the itihāsas and पुराणस्.
According to some versions, this vrata was taught by the sage पुलस्त्य to the king भीम who was the ड़थेर् of दमयन्ती, the wife of नल.
